'''Alice Jeanne LaDuke''' (born June 27, 1938) is an American mathematician who specialized in [[mathematical analysis]] and the [[history of mathematics]]. She was also a [[child actor|child actress]] who appeared in one film (''[[The Green Promise]]'').

==Early life and film career==
LaDuke was raised on a farm in [[Posey County, Indiana|Posey County]],{{r|vernon}} in southwest [[Indiana]]. Her parents were college-educated and an aunt who taught mathematics in [[Chicago]] frequently visited, bringing mathematics puzzles for LaDuke.{{r|oq}}

As a child, she was cast from a field of 12,000 [[4-H]] members to play a small part in ''[[The Green Promise]]'' (1948){{r|vernon}} as farm girl Jessie Wexford, the sister of [[Natalie Wood]]'s character's love interest.{{r|sullivan}} Wood and LaDuke shared a tutor who taught them both string games as well as their school curriculum.{{r|natasha}}

==Education==
LaDuke studied mathematics at [[DePauw University]] in the 1950s, and roomed with another mathematics major from Oregon, who showed her the state on summer camping trips.{{r|oq}}

She earned a master's degree in mathematics, but was unable to obtain a teaching position with it because the schools she applied to only hired men. She returned to Oregon in 1966 as a doctoral student at the [[University of Oregon]],{{r|oq}} and completed her Ph.D. in 1969 with a dissertation in mathematical analysis supervised by [[Kenneth A. Ross]] on ''E<sub>p</sub> Space: Essentially a Product of C<sub>p</sub> Spaces''.{{r|mgp}}

==Mathematics career==
After completing her doctorate, LaDuke spent the following thirty years as a faculty member of the department of mathematical sciences at [[DePaul University]].{{r|oq}} She retired in 2003.{{r|mathscifac}}

With [[Judy Green (mathematician)|Judy Green]], she is the author of ''[[Pioneering Women in American Mathematics|Pioneering Women in American Mathematics: The Pre-1940 PhD’s]]'' ([[American Mathematical Society]] and [[London Mathematical Society]], 2009).{{r|pwam}} An annual lecture series on Women in Mathematics, Science, and Technology at DePaul is named after her.{{r|field}}
